body.heading: A clock inside the stem
paragraphs: Tracking the Sun is called heliotropism, and in sunflowers it is driven by an internal daily clock rather than simple light-chasing. At night, the stem grows faster on its west side, swinging the head back to face east before dawn — the plant anticipates sunrise instead of merely reacting to it.

Experiments that moved sunflowers indoors under fixed lights found the plants kept swaying on their roughly 24-hour rhythm for days, and struggled when researchers imposed artificial days of the wrong length. The behaviour is timed from within.

body.heading: Why bother turning?
paragraphs: Facing the Sun warms the flower head, and warm heads attract more pollinating insects; east-facing heads can draw several times more bee visits than west-facing ones. Warmth also helps seeds develop. Interestingly, mature sunflower heads mostly stop tracking and settle facing east, keeping the warmth benefit.
Growth itself does the steering. No muscles, no nerves — just one side of the stem growing a little faster than the other, guided by a clock written into the plant's cells.

takeaway: Young sunflowers track the Sun using an internal clock that grows one side of the stem faster than the other.
